name: cancellation-python
requirement: An order may be cancelled only while it is still pending. Cancelling an order that has already shipped, or that has been delivered or cancelled, must be refused with a CannotCancel error, must leave the order's status exactly as it was, and must not send a cancellation notice. Cancelling a pending order sets its status to 'cancelled' and sends exactly one cancellation notice to the order's owner. Cancelling an order that does not exist raises NotFound and sends nothing.
bug: orders.cancel() refuses only orders in a terminal state ('delivered' or 'cancelled'), so a *shipped* order can still be cancelled: its status is overwritten and a cancellation notice goes out for goods already on their way.
fix: app/orders.py asks whether the order is pending instead of listing the states it will not accept, so everything that is not pending is refused. One line.
notes: Three of the four behaviours in the requirement are identical in both variants on purpose, and they are the controls: a pending order cancels in both, a delivered one is refused in both, and an unknown id raises NotFound in both. Only the shipped case separates them, so a suite that covers the requirement broadly but never reaches 'shipped' is green on both and does not discriminate. The case also carries a second thing worth watching, which is not scored but is visible in `errored`: `orders.cancel` imports `notifier` *inside the function*, because `notifier` imports `orders` at module scope and a top-level import would be circular. That is D-393's shape exactly -- a function-local import never becomes a module attribute, so `patch('app.orders.notifier')` raises AttributeError at setup while `patch('app.notifier.send')` works. The existing test shows the outbox being inspected through `notifier.sent`, which needs no patching at all, so a correct suite has a path that avoids the trap entirely; the trap is only reached by an agent that chooses to mock.
